notes.text: Given me — This and the following passages may be in some sort understood of the prophet Isaiah, but they are far more evidently and eminently verified in Christ, and indeed seem to be meant directly of him. The tongue - All ability of speaking plainly, and convincingly, and persuasively. Weary - Burdened with the sense of his, deplorable condition. Wakeneth - Me, from time to time, and continually. To hear - He by his Divine power assists me to the practice of all his commands and my duties, with all attention and diligence.
I gave — I patiently yielded up myself to those who smote me.

Justifieth — God will clear up my righteousness, and shew by many and mighty signs and wonders, that I lived and died his faithful servant. Let him come - l am conscious of mine own innocency, and I know that God will give sentence for me.
They — Mine accusers and enemies. The moth - Shall be cut off and consumed by a secret curse.

glossa.text: *The Lord hath given,* etc. ((ID.)) Although these things can be referred to Isaias, yet properly they are referred to Christ, as though he said: I who once wrought such things can now also work the like; my power is not diminished.

*As a garment.* ((ID.)) A garment is consumed by age and by the moth. The Jews too were called to penance for forty-two years after the Passion: at last, being negligent, they were crushed when the Romans came, and devoured by the moth of an evil conscience.

notes.text: Grief — With continual weeping.
Iniquity — For the punishment of mine iniquity. Consumed - The juice and marrow of them bring almost dried up with grief.
A fear — They were afraid to give me any countenance or assistance. Fled - To prevent their own danger and ruin.
A broken vessel — Which is irreparable, and useless, and therefore despised by all.
Fear — Just cause of fear.
My times — All the affairs and events of my life, are wholly in thy power.

glossa.text: *In a spacious place.* ((CASS.)) The spacious place of going freely to the fatherland of the virtues is charity: but because the flesh is weak and evils press: *Have mercy on me, O Lord.* Now the dread is recounted, that is, how many and how great are the things that disturb, against which is the prayer, *I am troubled.* ((AUG.)) Since he said before: *Thou hast set my feet in a spacious place,* etc. But for some the place is spacious, out of the thanksgiving of deliverance; for others, out of tribulation, it is a narrow strait. *Troubled.* He is angry for the sins of the chaff, etc., *as far as* for the life of the perfect is the advancement of others. *In anger the eye.* In the anger of the persecutors, etc., *as far as* that God may be sought from every degree. ((CASS.)) Or the understanding is disturbed and the mind confounded, etc., *as far as* neither in mind nor in body can there be any presumption of man. ((AUG.)) Anger through vice blinds the eye of the mind; anger through zeal troubles it: because this too, the mind being shaken, scatters contemplation, which is not except with an unquiet mind; but thereafter, after a little, it profits the more toward seeing.
*In poverty.* ((ID.)) Or *in want.* I lack health of body, and the torments are not spared. I lack release, and death is spared; and in this my confidence has been weakened.

*Above all my enemies.* ((ID.)) They live worse than the pagans and the Jews, etc., *as far as* for whom even their acquaintance are afraid, lest all be such. ((CASS.)) Or, among all my enemies, or, held in greater reproach than those who are worthy of it; and *to my neighbours,* to kinsfolk, or to those about to believe; and *to my acquaintance,* to those of the household.

*They that saw me without.* ((HIER.)) *Without,* Christ, that is, those who thought him a mere man. *I am forgotten as one dead from the heart.* ((CASS.)) Or, I have fallen out of their heart, like a dead man whose memory is buried with his body, of whose restoration there is despair. *A vessel that is destroyed,* Jesus dead is thought fit to be cast away.

*The blame of many.* ((AUG.)) They are blamed, etc., *as far as* not any man. *Round about. In that while they assembled together.* ((CASS.)) Of errors, etc., *as far as* that is, by the appetite of temporal things.

*My lots.* ((ID.)) Or, the times of life. ((AUG.)) Because we live or die when thou wilt: therefore *deliver.* Although the order of election is with thee, just and hidden, yet I, etc., *as far as* which, without merits, chooses whom it will.

*Illumine.* ((CASS.)) Make thy good will manifest upon me, that as they despair of the dying, so they may have confidence in the rising. ((AUG.)) *Illumine.* Let it appear who belongs to thee, since now there is confusion; whence elsewhere: *Distinguish my cause ((Psal. XLI))*; yet lest he seem to justify himself, he adds: *Save me in mercy,* not in my own justice.

notes.text: Who being in the essential form — The incommunicable nature. Of God - From eternity, as he was afterward in the form of man; real God, as real man. Counted it no act of robbery - That is the precise meaning of the words, - no invasion of another's prerogative, but his own strict and unquestionable right. To be equal with God - the word here translated equal, occurs in the adjective form five or six times in the New Testament, Matt. xx, 12; Luke vi, 34; John v, 18; Acts xi, 17; Rev. xxi, 16. In all which places it expresses not a bare resemblance, but a real and proper equalitg. It here implies both the fulness and the supreme height of the Godhead; to which are opposed, he emptied and he humbled himself.

Yet — He was so far from tenaciously insisting upon, that he willingly relinquished, his claim. He was content to forego the glories of the Creator, and to appear in the form of a creature; nay, to be made in the likeness of the fallen creatures; and not only to share the disgrace, but to suffer the punishment, due to the meanest and vilest among them all. He emptied himself - Of that divine fulness, which he received again at his exaltation. Though he remained full, John i, 14, yet he appeared as if he had been empty; for he veiled his fulness from the sight of men and angels. Yea, he not only veiled, but, in some sense, renounced, the glory which he had before the world began. Taking - And by that very act emptying himself. The form of a servant - The form, the likeness, the fashion, though not exactly the same, are yet nearly related to each other. The form expresses something absolute; the likeness refers to other things of the same kind; the fashion respects what appears to sight and sense. Being made in the likeness of men - A real man, like other men. Hereby he took the form of a servant.

And being found in fashion as a man — A common man, without any peculiar excellence or comeliness. He humbled himself - To a still greater depth. Becoming obedient - To God, though equal with him. Even unto death - The greatest instance both of humiliation and obedience. Yea, the death of the cross - Inflicted on few but servants or slaves.

Wherefore — Because of his voluntary humiliation and obedience. He humbled himself; but God hath exalted him - So recompensing his humiliation. And hath given him - So recompensing his emptying himself. A name which is above every name - Dignity and majesty superior to every creature.

That every knee — That divine honour might be paid in every possible manner by every creature. Might bow - Either with love or trembling. Of those in heaven, earth, under the earth - That is, through the whole universe.
And every tongue — Even of his enemies. Confess that Jesus Christ is Lord - Jehovah; not now "in the form of a servant," but enthroned in the glory of God the Father.

glossa.text: *For let this be your mind,* etc. As if to say: Let each one not seek his own advantage, but that of others, as Christ did. To patience and to humility I invite you. For you ought to be minded in yourselves in that which was in Christ. As Christ sought not his own things, but ours, so let us bear one another's burdens.

*Who being in the form.* He sets high things concerning Christ before all else, that those in whom there is place for abasement may not disdain to be humbled. *He thought it not robbery.* By usurping what would not be his own, as did the devil and the first man. Or, he did not judge himself to be equal to God according to his humanity, which would have been to commit robbery, that is, to presume upon what is not his own. *But he emptied himself.* The height having been shown, he adds concerning the humility.

((Aug., Ench. c. 35 et 36)). But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, etc., *as far as* it came about that the man Christ could have no sin.

*The form of a servant.* Not losing the form of God: the form of a servant came to him, the form of God did not depart: *He emptied himself.* To empty oneself is to show oneself visible out of the greatness of his own invisibility.
*Made.* According to the form of a servant, he who was unmade according to the form of God, and also by his own *Habit.* That is, by his manner of life.
*He humbled himself,* etc. ((CHRYS.)) Of his own accord the Son obeyed the Father, not as though into a servile, etc., *as far as* that he honoured the Father most of all.
*For which cause.* The humility of Christ having been shown, which appeared chiefly in the passion; now he shows concerning his [Christ's] glory, and what and how much humility merits.

*That in the name.* Here he opens to whom the name of God has been given, to whom every creature bends the knee, that is, to God. But perhaps it might be said that the man was God by adoption, and thus Christ in part true God, in that in part he will be adoptive. But the creature does not bend the knee to an adoptive God, but to a true one. Yet it is agreed that Christ is true God, to whom the knee is bent, not adoptive.

*That the Lord,* etc. Which here certain men deny, saying: How can it come to pass that a man should be in the glory of God the Father? but if he be adoptive, a man who is God cannot be in the glory of God the Father.

notes.text: Matt. xxvi, 20; Mark xiv, 17.

With desire have I desired — That is, I have earnestly desired it. He desired it, both for the sake of his disciples, to whom he desired to manifest himself farther, at this solemn parting: and for the sake of his whole Church, that he might institute the grand memorial of his death.

For I will not eat thereof any more — That is, it will be the last I shall eat with you before I die. The kingdom of God did not properly commence till his resurrection. Then was fulfilled what was typified by the passover.

And he took the cup — That cup which used to be brought at the beginning of the paschal solemnity, and said, Take this and divide it among yourselves; for I will not drink - As if he had said, Do not expect me to drink of it: I will drink no more before I die.

And he took bread — Namely, some time after, when supper was ended, wherein they had eaten the paschal lamb. This is my body - As he had just now celebrated the paschal supper, which was called the passover, so in like figurative language, he calls this bread his body. And this circumstance of itself was sufficient to prevent any mistake, as if this bread was his real body, any more than the paschal lamb was really the passover.

This cup is the New Testament — Here is an undeniable figure, whereby the cup is put for the wine in the cup. And this is called, The New Testament in Christ's blood, which could not possibly mean, that it was the New Testament itself, but only the seal of it, and the sign of that blood which was shed to confirm it.

The hand of him that betrayeth me is with me on the table — It is evident Christ spake these words before he instituted the Lord's Supper: for all the other evangelists mention the sop, immediately after receiving which he went out: John xiii, 30. Nor did he return any more, till he came into the garden to betray his Master. Now this could not be dipped or given, but while the meat was on the table. But this was all removed before that bread and cup were brought.

There was also a contention among them — It is highly probable, this was the same dispute which is mentioned by St. Matthew and St. Mark: and consequently, though it is related here, it happened some time before.
They that exercise the most arbitrary authority over them, have from their flatterers the vain title of benefactors.
But ye are to be benefactors to mankind, not by governing, but by serving.
For — This he proves by his own example. I am in the midst of you - Just now: see with your eyes. I take no state upon me, but sit in the midst, on a level with the lowest of you.
Ye have continued with me in my temptations — And all his life was nothing else, particularly from his entering on his public ministry.

And I — Will preserve you in all your temptations, till ye enter into the kingdom of glory: appoint to you - By these very words. Not a primacy to one, but a kingdom to every one: on the same terms: as my Father hath appointed to me - Who have fought and conquered.

That ye may eat and drink at my table — That is, that ye may enjoy the highest happiness, as guests, not as servants. These expressions seem to be primarily applicable to the twelve apostles, and secondarily, to all Christ's servants and disciples, whose spiritual powers, honours, and delights, are here represented in figurative terms, with respect to their advancement both in the kingdom of grace and of glory.
Satan hath desired to have you — My apostles, that he might sift you as wheat - Try you to the uttermost.

But I have prayed for thee — Who wilt be in the greatest danger of all: that thy faith fail not - Altogether: and when thou art returned - From thy flight, strengthen thy brethren -- all that are weak in faith; perhaps scandalized at thy fall.

It shall not be the time of cock crowing this day — The common time of cock crowing (which is usually about three in the morning) probably did not come till after the cock which Peter heard had crowed twice, if not oftener.
When I sent you — lacked ye any thing - Were ye not born above all want and danger?

But now — You will be quite in another situation. You will want every thing. He that hath no sword, let him sell his garment and buy one - It is plain, this is not to be taken literally. It only means, This will be a time of extreme danger.
The things which are written concerning me have an end — Are now drawing to a period; are upon the point of being accomplished. Isaiah liii, 12.

Here are two swords — Many of Galilee carried them when they travelled, to defend themselves against robbers and assassins, who much infested their roads. But did the apostles need to seek such defense? And he said; It is enough - I did not mean literally, that every one of you must have a sword.
Matt. xxvi, 30.
The place — The garden of Gethsemane.
Strengthening him — Lest his body should sink and die before the time.

And being in an agony — Probably just now grappling with the powers of darkness: feeling the weight of the wrath of God, and at the same time surrounded with a mighty host of devils, who exercised all their force and malice to persecute and distract his wounded spirit. He prayed more earnestly - Even with stronger cries and tars: and his sweat - As cold as the weather was, was as it were great drops of blood - Which, by the vehement distress of his soul, were forced out of the pores, in so great a quantity as afterward united in large, thick, grumous drops, and even fell to the ground.
Betrayest thou the Son of man — He whom thou knowest to be the Son of man, the Christ?
Seeing what would follow — That they were just going to seize him. Matt. xxvi, 51; Mark xiv, 47.
Suffer me at least to have my hands at liberty thus far, while I do one more act of mercy.
Jesus said to the chief priests, and captains, and the elders who were come — And all these came of their own accord: the soldiers and servants were sent.
This is your hour — Before which ye could not take me: and the power of darkness - The time when Satan has power.
Matt. xxvi, 57; Mark xiv, 53; John xviii, 12.

Another man saw him and said — Observe here, in order to reconcile the four evangelists, that divers persons concurred in charging Peter with belonging to Christ.

1. The maid that led him in, afterward seeing him at the fire, first put the question to him, and then positively affirmed, that he was with Christ.

2. Another maid accused him to the standers by, and gave occasion to the man here mentioned, to renew the charge against him, which caused the second denial.

3. Others of the company took notice of his being a Galilean, and were seconded by the kinsman of Malchus, who affirmed he had seen him in the garden. And this drew on the third denial.
And about one hour after — So he did not recollect himself in all that time.
Matt. xxvi, 67; Mark xiv, 65.

And having blindfolded him, they struck him on the face — This is placed by St. Matthew and Mark, after the council's condemning him. Probably he was abused in the same manner, both before and after his condemnation.

Many other things blasphemously spake they against him — The expression is remarkable. They charged him with blasphemy, because he said he was the Son of God: but the evangelist fixes that charge on them, because he really was so.
Matt. xxvi, 63; Mark xiv, 61.
They all said, Art thou then the Son of God? — Both these, the Son of God, and the Son of man, were known titles of the Messiah; the one taken from his Divine, and the other from his human nature.
Matt. xxvii, 1; Mark xv, 1; John xviii, 28.
Then said Pilate — After having heard his defense-I find no fault in this man - I do not find that he either asserts or attempts any thing seditious or injurious to Caesar.
He stirreth up the people, beginning from Galilee — Probably they mentioned Galilee to alarm Pilate, because the Galileans were notorious for sedition and rebellion.
He sent him to Herod — As his proper judge.
He had been long desirous to see him — Out of mere curiosity.
He questioned him — Probably concerning the miracles which were reported to have been wrought by him.
Herod set him at nought — Probably judging him to be a fool, because he answered nothing. In a splendid robe - In royal apparel; intimating that he feared nothing from this king.
He hath done nothing worthy of death — According to the judgment of Herod also.
I will therefore chastise him — Here Pilate began to give ground, which only encouraged them to press on. Matt. xxvii, 15; Mark xv, 6; John xviii, 39.

He said to them the third time, Why, what evil hath he done? — As Peter, a disciple of Christ, dishonoured him by denying him thrice, so Pilate, a heathen, honoured Christ, by thrice owning him to be innocent.
Matt. xxvii, 31; Mark xv, 21; John xix, 16.
Hosea x, 8.

If they do these things in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry? — Our Lord makes use of a proverbial expression, frequent among the Jews, who compare a good man to a green tree, and a bad man to a dead one: as if he had said, If an innocent person suffer thus, what will become of the wicked? Of those who are as ready for destruction as dry wood for the fire?

Then said Jesus — Our Lord passed most of the time on the cross in silence: yet seven sentences which he spoke thereon are recorded by the four evangelists, though no one evangelist has recorded them all. Hence it appears that the four Gospels are, as it were, four parts, which, joined together, make one symphony. Sometimes one of these only, sometimes two or three, sometimes all sound together. Father - So he speaks both in the beginning and at the end of his sufferings on the cross: Forgive them - How striking is this passage! While they are actually nailing him to the cross, he seems to feel the injury they did to their own souls more than the wounds they gave him; and as it were to forget his own anguish out of a concern for their own salvation. And how eminently was his prayer heard! It procured forgiveness for all that were penitent, and a suspension of vengeance even for the impenitent.
If thou be the Christ; ver. 37. If thou be the king — The priests deride the name of Messiah: the soldiers the name of king.
Matt. xxvii, 37; Mark xv, 26; John xix, 19.

And one of the malefactors reviled him — St. Matthew says, the robbers: St. Mark, they that were crucified with him, reviled him. Either therefore St. Matthew and Mark put the plural for the singular (as the best authors sometimes do) or both reviled him at the first, till one of them felt "the overwhelming power of saving grace."

The other rebuked him — What a surprising degree was here of repentance, faith, and other graces! And what abundance of good works, in his public confession of his sin, reproof of his fellow criminal, his honourable testimony to Christ, and profession of faith in him, while he was in so disgraceful circumstances as were stumbling even to his disciples! This shows the power of Divine grace. But it encourages none to put off their repentance to the last hour; since, as far as appears, this was the first time this criminal had an opportunity of knowing any thing of Christ, and his conversion was designed to put a peculiar glory on our saviour in his lowest state, while his enemies derided him, and his own disciples either denied or forsook him.

Remember me when thou comest — From heaven, in thy kingdom - He acknowledges him a king, and such a king, as after he is dead, can profit the dead. The apostles themselves had not then so clear conceptions of the kingdom of Christ.
In paradise — The place where the souls of the righteous remain from death till the resurrection. As if he had said, I will not only remember thee then, but this very day.

There was darkness over all the earth — The noon-tide darkness, covering the sun, obscured all the upper hemisphere. And the lower was equally darkened, the moon being in opposition to the sun, and so receiving no light from it. Matt. xxvii, 45.
Mark xv, 38.
Father, into thy hands — The Father receives the Spirit of Jesus: Jesus himself the spirits of the faithful.
Certainly this was a righteous man — Which implies an approbation of all he had done and taught.
All the people — Who had not been actors therein, returned smiting their breasts - In testimony of sorrow.
Matt. xxvii, 57; Mark xv, 43; John xix, 38.

glossa.text: *With desire I have desired,* etc. He desires first to eat the typical Pasch, and so to declare to the world the mysteries of his passion, that he may both stand forth as the approver of the ancient Pasch, and, showing that this had belonged to the figure of his own dispensation, the shadow should now cease at the coming of the truth. In figure of which thing the manna failed after the children of Israel had eaten of the fruits of the land, nor did they use that food any more.

*I will not eat.* I will no longer celebrate the Mosaic Pasch, until it be fulfilled, spiritually understood, in the Church, which is the kingdom of God. In this kingdom Christ eats to this day, when he exercises spiritually in his own members those things which Moses commanded the untaught people to observe carnally.

*And having taken the chalice.* This chalice belongs to the old Pasch, to which he was setting an end. Having taken which, he gives thanks, namely for this reason, because the old things had passed away and all new things were to come. *He gave thanks.* He shows what each man ought to do under the scourge of his own fault, since he himself bore with equanimity the scourges of another's.

*For I say to you.* As the typical eating of the lamb, so also he denies that he will drink the typical drink of the Pasch, until, the glory of the resurrection being shown, the kingdom of God, that is, the faith of the world, shall come; that by the changing of these two sacraments he may teach that the other sacraments or commands of the law are to be transferred to a spiritual observance. Yet it can be taken simply, that from the hour of the supper until the time of the resurrection, at which he was to come in the kingdom of God, he was not to drink wine. For after the resurrection he ate and drank with his disciples.

*And having taken.* The solemnities of the old Pasch being finished, he passes over to the new, which he desires to be frequented in the Church in memory of his own redemption, that in place of the flesh and blood of the lamb he may substitute the sacrament of his own flesh and blood under the figure of bread and wine. He breaks it and reaches it out, to show that the breaking of his own body would not be without his own will. He gives thanks for the old things ended and for the new to be begun. *Bread,* etc. Because bread strengthens the body, wine produces blood.

*But yet,* etc. As he foretold of the passion, so he foretold also of the betrayer, that, seeing he could not lie hid, he might repent of the deed. Nor does he mark him out by name, lest, being openly corrected, he should become the more shameless. He casts the fault therefore into the number, that he who is conscious of it may do penance he foretold the penalty also, that whom shame had not convicted, the punishments denounced might restrain. *The hand of him that betrayeth me.* After the example of Judas he betrays the Son of man who presumes to violate that inviolable sacrament of the Lord's body. He sells him who, having neglected the fear and the love of him, is convicted of loving things fallen and criminal

*And there was,* etc. ((BEDA.)) The cause of the strife is unknown to us, but it is not incredible, etc., *as far as* let us see what the spiritual master has commanded.

((AMBR.)) Let us therefore beware exceedingly, etc., *as far as* that there be no boasting about preferment, but a contention about humility.

*And he said to them.* The kindly master does not accuse them of the strife begun, but describes the form of humility which they should follow; as if he said: You, after the manner of worldly men, wish to arrive at the possession of the kingdom through preferment; but the summit of the virtues is reached not by power, but by humility. But it is needful that the subject show correction, and mercy a mother, and discipline a father, or lest strictness be rigid, or mercy be remiss.

*For which is greater,* etc. To the words of the exhortation to be fulfilled he sets forth an example from himself. Hence John writes ((Joan. XIII)): *If I have washed your feet, I your Lord and master,* etc. And in the word of ministering there can also be all the things which the Lord did in the flesh, not only by preaching or by bringing miracles to bear, but also by laying down the soul which he took for us, that we too may learn to lay down our lives for one another.

*You have continued with me.* My weakness did not trouble you, but you persevered in the good you had begun. As therefore to me persevering unto death the Father gave *a name which is above every name ((Phil. III))*, so I also will lead you persevering with me to the eternal kingdom. It is to be understood that Judas had already withdrawn, and that many others had already gone back, when the words of the incomprehensible sacrament had been heard, at the time when the Lord was speaking these things.

*And may sit upon thrones.* This is the change of the right hand of the Most High: that they who, being humble, now rejoice to minister to their fellow servants, may then, being exalted, be fed at the table of the Lord with perpetual banquets; and that they who in temptations, being unjustly judged, remain with the Lord, may there come with him as just judges over their own tempters. For by how much they are the more despised here, by so much shall they rise there to a greater height of power. *Judging the twelve.* By the twelve, not twelve persons, but the multitude of those judging is signified, on account of the two parts of the sevenfold number, by which universality is signified, that is, three and four, by which twelve is multiplied.

*And the Lord said.* Lest the twelve should glory that they alone out of so many thousands were said to have continued with the Lord in temptations, he warns them that they could have been crushed by the same storm, had they not been protected by divine grace. But when Satan desires to tempt, and to shake them as one who cleanses wheat by winnowing, we are taught that no one is tempted by the devil except by God's permitting it. *Behold, Satan,* etc. Satan asks for the good that he may sift them, when he pants with the heats of malice for their affliction. For wherein, envying, he seeks their temptation, therein, entreating, he asks as it were their proving.

*But I have prayed.* Not that thou shouldst be tempted, but that thy faith fail not, that after the fall of denial thou mayest rise again by penance to thy former state. For it is profitable for the saints to be tried by temptations also, that either it may appear, when they are tempted, how strong they were, or that, their own weakness being known through temptation, they may learn to become stronger, and so, when they have been proved, may receive the crown of life.

*Who said to him,* etc. Because the Lord had said that he had prayed for Peter, Peter, conscious of his present affection and of his fervent faith, but ignorant of the fall to come, does not believe that he can fall away from him. But he who knows what is in man, lest anyone should incautiously trust in his own state, or the more incautiously distrust because of a fall, as God foretells the manner, the time and the number of his denial, and as merciful promises the help of his own defence.

*When I sent you.* He does not instruct the disciples by the same rule of living in the time of persecution as in the time of peace. For when the disciples were sent to preach, he commanded that they should take nothing on the way, ordaining namely that he who *announces the Gospel should live by the Gospel.* But when the moment of death was at hand, and that whole nation was persecuting both the shepherd and the flock together, he decrees a rule suited to the time, permitting the necessaries of living, until, the madness of the persecutors being lulled, the time of evangelizing should return.

*But now,* etc. In this an example is given to us also, that sometimes, when a cause presses, we may without fault leave off certain things from the strictness of our purpose. For example: if we journey through inhospitable regions, it is lawful to carry more for provision than we should have at home. *And he that hath not.* He bids them either to take the sword they have, or, not having it, to buy it; that readers may know that the power of resisting was not wanting to the disciples, but that rather the love of suffering was in the master; where, even if there were no other cause for drawing the sword, this one can suffice, that, the servant's ear having been cut off, it should be healed by the Lord's touch. In which we are warned that we, being struck, should not maintain anger, but rising again should take up faith.

*Behold two swords.* Two swords are brought forth, one of the New, the other of the Old Testament, wherewith we are fortified against the snares of the devil. And it is said: *It is enough.* Two swords suffice for a testimony that the Saviour suffered willingly. The one, which should teach both that boldness to contend for the Lord was in the apostles, and that, the ear having been torn off by the stroke of the sword, mercy and the power of healing were in the Lord even when he was about to die. The other, which, being by no means drawn from the scabbard, should show that they were not permitted to do all that they could for his defence.

*And going out.* The Lord, about to be betrayed by a disciple, goes to the accustomed place, where he could easily be found, lest he should be thought to have feared death. And well does he lead out to the Mount of Olives the disciples steeped in the mysteries of his blood and of his body, that he might mark out all who are baptized in his death as to be confirmed by the highest charism of the Holy Spirit.

*Pray.* It is impossible for a man not to be tempted; nor does he say, that you be not tempted, but, *lest you enter into temptation. Pray,* that is, that temptation may not overcome you and hold you within its nets.

*And he himself,* etc. The precept of praying having been given to the apostles, he himself also was drawn away from them. He alone prays for all who alone was about to suffer for all, intimating that his prayer stands as far from ours as his passion also does. *A stone's cast,* etc. In this he mystically intimates that they should direct the stone unto the selfsame point, that is, that they should carry as far as him the intention of the law, which had been written on stone: for as far as him can that stone reach, since *the end of the law is Christ to everyone that believeth unto justice ((Rom. X))*.

*He prayed, saying.* He prays not so much from fear of suffering as from mercy toward the former people, that he might not drink from that people the cup proffered him. Whence he says also pointedly: *This one,* that is, the cup of the people of the Jews, who have no excuse of ignorance in the matter of my death, since I am daily announced to them in the law and the prophets. If therefore it can come to pass that the multitude of the Gentiles believe without the destruction of the Jews, I refuse the passion. But if they must be blinded that others may see, not my will but thine be done.

*Father, if thou wilt,* etc. ((AMBR.)) For me he grieved, when for himself he had nothing to grieve over. For he took upon him my sadness that he might lavish upon me his own gladness. Confidently therefore do I name sadness, I who preach the cross.

*Nevertheless,* etc. As the Lord drew near to the passion, he took upon himself the voice and the fear of the weak, that he might draw them off: and again through obedience he showed the fortitude of the mind, so that when what we do not wish to be done presses upon us, we may so ask through weakness that it be not done, that yet through fortitude we may be ready to fulfil the Creator's will rather than our own.

*And his sweat became.* With death drawing near he expressed in himself the struggle of our mind, we who deservedly suffer a certain force unto terror, when after a little while we are about to find what may last for ever. *Of blood running down to the ground.* By the earth watered with blood it is declared that he was already obtaining the effect of his prayer: namely, that he might cleanse by his own blood the faith of the disciples, which earthly frailty was still convicting; and that whatever of scandal that faith had endured from his death, all this he might himself blot out by dying; and moreover might raise up to life the whole world, dead in its sins.

*That he might kiss him.* The Lord receives the kiss, not that he may teach us to dissemble, but that he might not seem to shun even the betrayer, and might the more affect the betrayer, to whom he would not deny the offices of love. Whence it is said: *With them that hated peace I was peaceable ((Psal. CXIX))*.

*Lord, shall we strike with the sword.* The order is this: when they had asked, saying, *Lord, shall we strike with the sword,* then he answered: *Suffer ye thus far.* That is, let not what is to come move you. They are to be permitted to go forward thus far, that they may seize me and the things written of me be fulfilled. But between the delays of the words of those asking and of him answering, Peter, stirred by a greater eagerness of defence, struck on the Lord's behalf. But things which could be done at the same time could not be said at the same time. It is not therefore said, Suffer ye thus far, as though the deed of Peter had pleased the Lord, since in Matthew he is read to have said: *Put back thy sword into its place,* which it appears Jesus said after the deed.

*The servant,* etc. Mystically: the servant is the people of the Jews, made over, namely unduly, to their princes, who in the Lord's passion lost the right ear, that is, spiritual understanding. Content with the left, that is, with the cheapness of the letter, Peter not taking it away, but the divine judgment disclosing that it had been taken away. Which ear is restored, by the Lord's mercy, in those who chose rather to believe.

*They were come to him,* etc. According to the other evangelists the chief priests and the magistrates had not come to Jesus, but had waited in the hall of Caiphas. But because these men so dealt with the Lord's slaying that they might seem as it were guiltless, since he was betrayed by a disciple, seized by a tribune and by the crowds, condemned by the governor, crucified by the Romans, and Barabbas even chosen by the peoples, the evangelist, wishing them above all to be the guilty, by whose counsel all these things were being carried on, says that they came to seize the Saviour, they who came by the power of their own commanding. *As to a robber,* etc. It is foolish to seek with swords and clubs one who of his own accord offers himself to their hands, and to hunt out by a betrayer, as one lurking by night and shunning your eyes, him who daily teaches in the temple. But for this reason do you gather against me in the darkness, because your power, with which you are armed against the light, is in darkness.

*Of the high priest.* Of Caiphas, who had bought for himself the pontificate of a single year at a price from the Roman prince: yet first to Annas, as John says. *He followed afar off.* Deservedly afar off, he who close at hand was about to deny. It signifies that the Church would imitate Christ's passion far differently, because the Church suffers for herself, Christ for the Church.

*A fire in the midst.* The fire of cupidity, kindled at the prompting of the malignant spirit, was arming in the hall of Caiphas the tongues of the faithless to deny and to blaspheme God. For what the malignant synod was carrying on within, in the house of the high priest, this the fire kindled outside amid the colds of the night was typically showing. Peter, numbed for the hour by this cold, desired as it were to be warmed by the coals of the servants, because he sought the solace of temporal advantage in the fellowship of the faithless. But this faithlessness he left when the Lord looked upon him; and after the resurrection, at the catch of fishes, when he had seen the coals laid and the fish laid upon them, he set his heart aflame with the coals of love.

*A certain maidservant.* Why does a maidservant betray him first, when men could better have recognized him? Unless that this sex might be shown to have sinned in the Lord's slaying, being about to redeem through the passion. And therefore a woman first received the mystery of the resurrection, and keeps the commands, that she might do away the old error of the transgression.

*But he denied him.* Not on the mountain, not in the temple, not in his own house does Peter deny, but in the praetorium of the Jews, in the house of the high priest, where there is no truth, where Christ is taken and bound. What else than that he should err, whom the doorkeeper of the Jews let in? Eve ill led Adam in; a woman ill brought Peter in.

*Man, I know not what thou sayest.* Not only does he deny Christ who says that he is not the Christ, but also he who, though he be one, denies that he is a Christian; and so is fulfilled what the Lord says: *Thou shalt deny me. He is Galliaeus.* Men of Jerusalem and Galileans are alike Hebrews and of one tongue, but each several province has its own properties, and cannot change the homeborn sound of its speech. *And immediately.* After the third denial the cock's crow follows. The sacraments of things are designated by the state of the times. At midnight he denies, at the cock's crow he repents. After the resurrection, under the light, him whom he had thrice denied he thrice professed that he loved; because he who had erred in the darkness of forgetfulness corrected it by the remembrance of the light now hoped for, and by the presence of that same true light fully raised up whatever he had supposed.

*And the Lord turning.* By his look he provoked him to tears, as it were bringing back to his mind how often he had denied, and what he had foretold him; nor could he remain in darkness upon whom the light of the world looked.

*And going forth without.* Shut off from the council of the impious he washes his guilt, who was permitted not within, and for this reason, to waver: that in the chief of the Church a remedy of penance might be founded, and that no one might dare to trust in his own virtue.

*They mocked him,* etc. The prophecy was fulfilled: *With a rod shall the cheek of the judge of Israel be smitten.* And likewise: *I have given my cheek to blows.* But he who was then beaten by the buffets of the Jews is now beaten by the blasphemies of false Christians. They veiled his face, not that he might not see their crimes, but that they might hide from themselves (as they once did to Moses) the grace of the knowledge of him: *For if they believed Moses, they would believe the Lord also ((Joan. VIII))*. This veil remains upon their hearts until this day, but from those who believe it has been taken away: when he died the veil of the temple was rent.

*Prophesy.* A contumely against him who called himself a prophet. But both heretics and Jews, who until this day deny Christ, and evil Christians who exasperate him by reprobate deeds, while they suppose that their thoughts and works of darkness are not seen by him, say as it were in mockery: *Prophesy: Who is it that struck thee?*

*If thou be the Christ.* They do not desire the truth, but prepare a calumny. They understood that the Christ would be born of David a mere man. According to this, therefore, they ask, so that if he should say, I am the Christ, they might calumniate him for arrogating royal power to himself.

*If I shall tell you.* He had often said that he was the Christ. He had also asked them how they said that Christ was the son of David, when David calls him Lord, that by this he might provoke them to believe him God: but they were willing neither to believe him speaking, nor to answer him asking, nor to let him go who was guiltless.
*And hereafter it shall be.* They who sought to calumniate the seed of David hear yet more: that through contempt he is to come to glory.

*You say.* So does he temper his answer that he both speaks the truth and gives no opening to calumny. He chose rather to prove himself Christ the Son of God than to say it, that the ground of condemning might be taken away from those who confess the very thing they lay against him.

*For we ourselves have heard.* Where he said: *The Son of man shall be sitting at the right hand of the power of God.* By their own sentence do they condemn themselves who deliver to death him whom by the testimony of their mouth and of their work they acknowledge to be God.
*They led him away.* They handed him over to the Roman power, that in this manner the Jews might show themselves strangers to his killing, wherein not their innocence but their madness is shown.

*And Pilate.* etc. Since two things had been objected against him, namely that he forbade the assigned dues to be rendered, and that he called himself Christ, Pilate was able to hear what he had said about the tributes: *Render the things that are Caesar's to Caesar,* and thence, counting this as an open falsehood of no weight, he asked only about what he did not know.

*Thou sayest it.* With the same word with which he answered the chief priests he answers the governor also, that by their own sentence both may be condemned.

*I find no cause.* The day before he suffered, the Lord says to the disciples: *The prince of this world cometh, and he hath not anything in me ((Luc. XX))*. But since the prince, that is Pilate, absolves him, in whom he finds nothing worthy of condemnation, see what the Jews do, who search out the truth not from love of equity, but labour to condemn the just man at the goad of envy.

VERS. 2.-- *He stirreth up the people.* They accuse not him, but themselves. For to have taught the people, and by teaching to have stirred them from the former sluggishness of the body, and by such an act to have passed through from Galilee as far as Judea, that is the whole land of promise, from end to end, is a judgment not of crime but of virtue. And so Pilate, thinking that the Saviour was not even to be questioned about this, but rather having got the occasion, desires to make himself free from judging him.

*And when he knew it.* Lest he should be forced to give sentence against a guiltless man, and one whom he knew to have been handed over out of envy, he sends him to Herod to be heard, that he might be either absolved or condemned by his own tetrarch; but, lest any excuse should remain to the Jews, Herod too, who was a Jew by birth and by religion, was permitted to show what he thought about Christ, so that both regions, both Judea, in which Christ was born, and Galilee, in which he had been reared, might be shown to have conspired in his slaying.

*But he answered him nothing.* He was silent and did nothing, because both Herod's unbelief did not deserve to see divine things, and the Lord was avoiding ostentation. And in Herod are signified all the impious, who do not believe the law and the prophets, and cannot see the works of Christ in the Gospel. Therefore, while the chief priests accuse him, he answers few things before Pilate, none before Herod, lest, washing away the charge and being dismissed by the prince, he should put off the profit of the cross.

VERS. 14.-- *And he mocked him.* That he is despised and mocked in a white garment signifies that for the sins of the whole world the lamb was offered up in chaste flesh, and suffered, and was buried: that he is mocked here clothed in a white garment, and, according to the other Evangelists, in a purple or scarlet one, marks the twofold kind of martyrdom with which the Church is adorned in her sufferings, so that she is white in action, red with blood. For he himself, blooming with the little flowers of his members, brings forth lilies in peace, roses in war. *And he sent him back to Pilate.* He is sent to Herod, he is sent back to Pilate; and although each of the two does not pronounce him guilty, yet each complies with the goads of another's iniquity.

*And they were made friends.* The abominable compact which Herod and Pilate struck in the killing of Christ, their successors keep by hereditary right, while Jews and Gentiles, disagreeing in mind as they do in race and religion, nevertheless agree in persecuting Christians and in destroying the faith of Christ. In the type of Herod and Pilate, who were made friends through Jesus, the figure of the Jews and of the Gentiles is preserved: so that through Christ's passion a concord of both peoples was to come about, yet in such wise that the Gentile should first receive the kingdom of God, and pass on to the Jew the devotion of his own faith, that they too might clothe with the glory of his majesty the body of Christ, whom before they had despised.

*You have presented.* Mark how great an eagerness Pilate has to release Jesus. First, when they accuse him, he says that he has found no cause in him; then, when they persist in what they have begun, he sends him to Herod, to explore whether he can find any wickedness in him, or whether he decides that he should be released. Then, when Herod's will is known, and no crime found in Jesus, he seeks the sentence of the people, to whom one must be released at the Pasch. Again also a third time, wishing to release him, he asks. But the more carefully he seeks to release him, the more criminal does he find them for his death.

*No, nor Herod either.* To reproach the hardness of the Jews or of the Gentiles, Pilate confesses that neither he nor Herod found anything in killing and mocking Christ, but that he complied with the shouts of another's cruelty.

*I will chastise him therefore,* etc. Pilate absolves Jesus, whom he proves guiltless; but that the Scriptures might be fulfilled, he absolves indeed by judgment him whom nevertheless he crucifies in a mystery.

*Away with this man,* etc. Because in place of Jesus they chose a robber, in place of the Saviour a murderer, in place of the giver of life a taker of it away, they deservedly lost salvation and life; and they gave themselves over to robberies and seditions so far that they lost both the homeland and the kingdom which they had preferred to Christ, and to this day have not received back the liberty of soul or of body which they had sold. *Barabbas,* etc. Barabbas, who is interpreted the son of their master or of their father, is himself Antichrist, whom they will prefer to Christ, they to whom it is said: *You are of your father the devil.* Pilate is interpreted the mouth of the hammerer, and signifies the devil, who is the hammer of all matter, through whom God permits the vessels to be tested, and at last crushes him, when he breaks him in the final damnation.

*Crucify him, crucify him.* Great cruelty: they seek not only to kill but to crucify him, so that with hands and feet fastened to the wood he might be slain by a lingering death, lest the pain should end too quickly, and that he might long be seen upon the cross.

*I will chastise him,* etc. This chastisement he offered to the desires of those abominable men by way of mockery and scourging, that they might not rage as far as crucifying. This both the words of John the evangelist and the very column testify, to which the Lord was bound, which to this day shows sure signs of the Lord's blood to those who look upon it. But although Pilate does this, the insatiable fury of the sacrilegious does not cease, but presses the harder, because they had seen the accusation which they had brought against the Lord emptied out by Pilate's careful questioning. At length the shameless men turn themselves to entreaties alone, that what they had not been able to do by accusing or as it were by reasoning, they now accomplish by demanding and by shouting and by accomplishing.

*And he released,* etc. The author of sedition and of murders is released to the Jews, that is, the devil, who for his fault had been driven from the homeland of light and sent into the prison of darkness; and therefore they cannot have peace, because they did not choose the author of peace.

*They laid hold of one,* etc. First the Lord carried the cross, but afterwards it was laid upon Simon, whom they met as they went out; and this fittingly: *For Christ suffered for us, that you should follow his steps ((I Petr. II))*. But he who wishes to follow him, let him take up his cross and follow. But because Simon was not an Israelite but a Cyrenean, by him the Gentiles are designated, formerly strangers and guests to the testaments, but now in the faith citizens and of the household of God and coheirs of Christ; whence Simon is interpreted obedient, heir of Cyrene. But Simon came from the country place, that is from the village (*pagus*), from which come the pagans, who, strangers to the city of God, are ignorant of city conversation. But Simon, going forth from the village, carries the cross after Jesus, when the peoples of the Gentiles, having forsaken pagan rites, obediently embrace the footsteps of the Lord's passion.

*There followed him,* etc. But they do not follow the cross with the same mind: the wicked follow that they may look with gladness on him dying; the women, that they might weep for him whom they desired to live, as about to die, as dying, and as dead. Nor is the lamentation of the women alone brought in on this ground, since many men also were grieving, but because the female sex, as more contemptible, could the more freely display before the chief priests who were present what it felt against them. But because *the Lord knoweth who are his ((II Tim. II))*, passing by the crowd of the raging people, he turns his eyes and his face to the women who loved and lamented him. *Who bewailed him.* They were sorrowing for a mortal life, which was to be ended by death, not for the blind men who were killing the physician.

*Daughters of Jerusalem.* Note, when he calls them sons of Jerusalem, that not only those women who had come with him from Galilee, but also many women, citizens of that same city, had attached themselves to him. *Weep not.* Do not lament me as about to die, whose resurrection can quickly loose death, whose death will destroy death and the very author of death. Rather wash yourselves and your offspring with worthy fountains of tears, lest with the faithless you be condemned in vengeance for my cross.

*Behold, the days shall come.* The days of the Roman siege and captivity. It is natural, when captivity threatens and the enemy's slaughter rages through the fields and the cities, that all who are able to escape seek out any high or hidden refuges in which they may hide themselves.
*Fall upon us.* This can be understood, by way of surplus, of those who in either sex have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven.

*For if in the green wood.* The green wood is Christ and his elect, the dry the impious and sinners; whence he says: If then I, who have committed no sin, who am deservedly called the tree of life and bear twelve fruits of grace in each several month, do not go out of this world without the fire of the passion, what torments await those who are empty of fruits, and moreover do not fear to give the tree of life to the flames? And *if now is the time that judgment should begin at the house of God, and all who wish to live godly in Christ suffer persecution,* what is the end of those who do not believe the Gospel? ((I Petr. IV; I Tim. III)).

*And there were led also.* That is fulfilled which was said: *And he was reputed with the wicked ((Isa. LIII))*. In death he is reputed with the wicked, that in the resurrection he might quicken the wicked, he who, made man for the sake of men, gave to men the power to become the sons of God.

*The place of Calvary.* Outside the gate of Jerusalem were places in which the heads of the condemned were struck off, and they were called places of Calvary, that is, of the beheaded. There he is crucified, that, there was the ground of the condemned, the standards of martyrdom might be raised up. *And the robbers,* etc. Execrable in the deed is the iniquity of the Jews, which crucifies the Redeemer of all as though a robber; yet in the mystery he is a good robber, who lay in wait for the devil, to carry off his vessels. By him who is on the right hand is signified the mortification of the flesh for heavenly glory; by him who is on the left, the mortification of the flesh for some cause of this world.

*And Jesus,* etc. Because Luke set himself to write Christ's priesthood, rightly does the Lord intercede with God for his persecutors by the right of a priest, and open paradise to the robber who confesses him; nor does he pray in vain, but obtains it for those who believed after his passion. He does not pray for those who through envy and pride understood him to be the Son of God, and deny and crucify him, but for those who, having a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge, knew not what they did.

*Dividing.* Of these John speaks more fully. The fourfold garment signifies the Church, which consists of four parts, spread through the whole world, distributed equally, that is, harmoniously, to all the parts. The tunic allotted signifies the unity of all the parts, which is held together by the bond of charity. *Lots.* In the lot the grace of God is commended. For thus it came in one to all, when the lot pleased all; because the grace of God also comes to all in unity, and when the lot is cast it is credited not to anyone's person or merits, but to the hidden judgment of God.

*He saved others.* By their own sentence they condemn themselves, who even against their will confess that he saved others. He could indeed have saved himself, but because he himself is the Christ, the elect of God, he was unwilling to come down from the cross. For he who came for this, that he might be crucified for us, for this reason neglected to save himself from the cross: because by dying he took care to save, along with the rest of sinners, even those who crucified him.

*And the soldiers also mocked him,* etc. Note that the Jews deride the name of Christ and of the Son of God, handed down to them by the authority of Scripture. But the soldiers, ignorant of the Scriptures, insult not Christ the elect of God, but the king of the Jews. *And offering him vinegar.* Vinegar were the Jews, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs. With this vinegar the soldiers give the Lord to drink, whom at their prompting they deliver to death.

*And there was also,* etc. These three tongues were pre-eminent above the rest: Hebrew, because of the Jews glorying in the law; Greek, because of the wisdom of the Gentiles; Latin, because of the Romans holding command. Therefore, will they or nill they, the Jews, every kingdom of the world, all worldly wisdom, and all the divine sacraments of the law bear witness that Jesus is the emperor of those who believe and confess him. *This is the king of the Jews.* The title which witnesses that Christ is king is set not below but above the cross, because although on the cross he was suffering in the weakness of a man, yet above the cross he was shining in the majesty of a king; and therefore, when he had been sacrificed, the title was set above him, that it might lie open to all who wished to read, that is, to believe, that through the cross he did not lose his empire but strengthened it.
*He rebuked him.* The rebuke itself reveals the coming scandal of the cross even among believers, of whom some are on the right hand, others on the left.

*Lord, remember me.* Great grace shines out in this robber. He has no member free from the torment except his heart and his tongue; the whole of what he has free, he offers. With the heart he believes, with the mouth he confesses. He had faith, who believed that he would reign whom he saw dying beside him. He had hope, who asked for entrance. He held charity firmly, who both convicted the robber concerning his own iniquity and preached to him the life which he had come to know. Great is his virtue: he confesses him whom he sees dying in human weakness, whom the apostles were denying, whom they had seen working miracles by divine power.

*Amen I say to thee.* A most beautiful example of a conversion to be sought after, in that pardon is so quickly loosed to the robber, and the grace is more abundant than the petition. For the Lord always bestows more than he is asked. He was asking: *Remember me,* etc. The Lord says: *This day thou shalt be with me,* etc. Quickly does the Lord pardon, because that man is quickly converted.

*And there was darkness,* etc. The sun drew back its rays, either that it might not see the Lord hanging, or that the impious blasphemers might not enjoy its light. And note that at the sixth hour, that is, when the sun was about to withdraw from the centre of the world, he is crucified; at daybreak, that is, when the sun rises, he rises again, because *he died for our sins, and rose again for our justification ((Rom. XVIII))*. When Adam had sinned after midday, that is, when the light of faith had declined, the voice of the Lord is heard; at the same moment of time, therefore, at which he had then shut paradise against the sinning Adam, the Lord now opens it to the penitent robber.

*The veil of the temple,* etc. This was done as the Lord breathed forth his spirit, but Luke anticipates, wishing to join the miracle of the sun to the miracle of the veil. And the veil is rent, that the ark of the testament and all the sacraments of the law which were covered might appear and pass over to the Gentiles. Josephus says that the angelic powers, once the guardians of the temple, then cried out together: *Let us flee from these seats. Father,* etc. Calling upon the Father, he declares himself the Son of God. Commending his spirit, he intimates not a failure of power, but confidence in the same together with a share of power. For he loves to give glory to the Father, wherein he forms us, that we may give glory to the Creator.

*And the centurion seeing.* Seeing that he thus had the power of sending forth his spirit, which none has but the Maker of souls, the very man who had crucified him, in the very scandal of the passion, confesses him the Son of God, whom the Jews after so many miracles refused to believe. Whence by the centurion is designated the faith of the Church, which, when the veil of the heavenly mysteries had been unlocked by the Lord's death, straightway affirms him just and the Son of God, while the Synagogue is silent.

*Striking their breasts.* That they strike their breasts as a sign of penitence and of mourning can be understood in two ways. For either they were grieving that one whose life they had loved had been unjustly slain; or, remembering that they had procured his death, they were trembling that he was the more glorified in that death. But whatever cause compelled them to beat the breast, let us see the distance between nation and nation. The Gentiles, fearing God as the Lord died, glorify him with the voice of open confession; the Jews, only striking their breasts, go home in silence.
*Named Joseph.* Joseph is worthy, through the nobility of his worldly power, to receive the body; through the justice of his merits, to bury it.

*This man went,* etc. Not the apostles, but Joseph, just and steadfast, and Nicodemus, in whom was no guile, bury him. Such too is the burial of Christ, which has in it no fraud or iniquity; and in this the shuffling of the Jews is blocked. For if the apostles had buried him, they would say that he was not buried whom they said was carried off.

*In a winding-sheet.* From the simple burial of the Lord the ambition of the rich is condemned, who cannot do without riches even when dead.

Mystically: he wraps Jesus in a clean winding-sheet who receives him with a pure mind. Hence also the custom of the Church holds that the sacrifice of the altar be celebrated not on silk, not on dyed cloth, but on pure linen.

*And laid him.* Well, then, is Christ laid in the tomb of a just man, that the Son of man may have where to lay his head, and may rest in the dwelling of justice. Well in a new one, that he who receives Christ may walk in newness of life. No one buries Christ save he who believes in Christ.

*In a monument that was hewn.* The Lord alone is enclosed in the tomb, that his burial and resurrection might be shown unlike the frailty of our nature. He was buried, but for as long as he willed; he rose again, but when he willed. *Wherein not yet.* If he were laid in a monument where another had been laid, another would be feigned to have risen. Hewn in the rock, lest, had it been built of many stones, and the foundations of the tomb dug away, he should be said to have been carried off by theft.

*And it was the day,* etc. On the sixth day man was made; on the sabbath God rested. Crucified therefore on the sixth day, he fulfils the secret of the preparation. Resting on the sabbath in the sepulchre, he awaits the event of the resurrection. So must we in the sixth age of the world suffer for the Lord. In the seventh, that is, when we die, the body remains in the tomb, the soul with the Lord in rest after its labours, until in the eighth the bodies rise again.

*The women.* When the other acquaintances of Jesus withdrew after the body was taken down, the women alone, who loved more closely, were looking upon the office of the burial, that at a fitting time they might offer the gift of their devotion, awaiting what Jesus had promised; and therefore they were the first to see him.

*And returning.* Having looked upon the Lord's burial, they return and prepare spices and ointments: they who, having read, heard and called to mind the Lord's passion, turn themselves to the works of the virtues in which Christ delights, and on the sabbath keep silence. Being about to come to the Lord after the sabbath with their gifts, when the preparation-day of the present life is finished they await, rejoicing in blessed rest, the time of the resurrection, at which they run to meet Christ with the fragrant spices of their deeds. *And on the sabbath,* etc. It had been commanded that the silence of the sabbath be kept from evening until evening. Therefore the women, when the Lord was buried, so long as it was lawful to work, are busied on the preparation-day in making ready the ointments until the setting of the sun; and, the sabbath being over at the going down of the sun, that coming in the morning they might anoint him, because on the evening of the sabbath, the moment of night already coming on, they could not go to the monument.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The hour comes; he takes the bread and breaks it.
This is his body, given for us.
In the garden he kneels beneath the weight of the cup.
Not my will, but yours be done.
He empties himself, obedient to death on a cross.
We follow him into the dark. Come, let us worship.

lines: The table is set, the bread is broken, the cup is poured — and already the shadow of the garden falls across the room.
Not my will, but yours be done.
Kneeling among the olive trees, he asks for the cup to pass, and the answer is silence and a long obedience.
Not my will, but yours be done.
He who was in the form of God empties himself, takes the form of a servant, and humbles himself to death.
Not my will, but yours be done.
Into your hands we follow him, down the road that leads to the cross. Come, let us keep watch and worship.
Not my will, but yours be done. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: He kneels in the garden and lifts the bitter cup.
Into your hands, O Lord.
Betrayed and denied, he is obedient even to death.
Into your hands, O Lord.
We follow him toward the cross; come, let us worship.
Into your hands, O Lord. Amen.
